claim: Human pyramidal cell to fast-spiking interneuron connections have similar quantal sizes compared to rats.
source: Multiple probability fluctuation analysis of human and rat unitary EPSCs fails to show a significant difference in quantal size (q, human: 40.2 ± 14.9 fC, n = 10; rat: 29.6 ± 13.3 fC, n = 12; p = 0.11, MW U-test)
evidence: Supported by MPFA experimental data showing no significant difference in quantal size between species (p = 0.11), presented in Figure 2F.

claim: Human pyramidal cell to fast-spiking interneuron connections have 4-times more functional release sites compared to rats.
source: the Nfrs in human is substantially larger compared to rats (human: 20.5 ± 15.4, n = 10; rat: 4.7 ± 2.3, n = 12; p < 0.001, MW U-test)
evidence: Supported by MPFA experimental data showing statistically significant difference in Nfrs between species (p < 0.001), presented in Figure 2F.

claim: Human and rat pyramidal cell to fast-spiking interneuron connections are mediated on average by three synaptic contacts.
source: These connections were mediated on average by three synaptic contacts in both species.
evidence: Supported by light microscopy reconstruction data showing similar number of contacts (human: 3.3 ± 1.5, n = 9; rat: 2.9 ± 1.5, n = 15; p = 0.36).

claim: Each presynaptic active zone contains 6.2 release sites in human.
source: Each presynaptic active zone (AZ) contains 6.2 release sites in human
evidence: Calculated from the ratio of mean Nfrs to mean Nlm (20.5/3.3 ≈ 6.2).

claim: Each presynaptic active zone contains 1.6 release sites in rats.
source: Each presynaptic active zone (AZ) contains 6.2 release sites in human, but only 1.6 in rats.
evidence: Calculated from the ratio of mean Nfrs to mean Nlm (4.7/2.9 ≈ 1.6).

claim: An active zone harbors 4 docked vesicles in human.
source: EM tomography showed that an AZ harbors 4 docked vesicles in human
evidence: Supported by electron microscopy data showing 4.2 ± 2.2 docked vesicles per AZ in human (n = 21).

claim: An active zone harbors only a single docked vesicle in rats.
source: EM tomography showed that an AZ harbors 4 docked vesicles in human, but only a single one in rats.
evidence: Supported by electron microscopy data showing 1.3 ± 0.8 docked vesicles per AZ in rats (n = 18).

claim: A Katz's functional release site occupies ~0.012 μm2 in the human presynaptic active zone.
source: a Katz's functional release site occupies ~0.012 μm2 in the human presynaptic AZ
evidence: Calculated from the mean AZ area (0.077 μm2) divided by the mean number of release sites per AZ (6.2).

claim: A Katz's functional release site occupies ~0.025 μm2 in the rat presynaptic active zone.
source: a Katz's functional release site occupies ~0.012 μm2 in the human presynaptic AZ and ~0.025 μm2 in the rat.
evidence: Calculated from the mean AZ area (0.041 μm2) divided by the mean number of release sites per AZ (1.6).

claim: Human unitary EPSCs have significantly larger mean amplitude compared to rats.
source: with a significantly larger mean amplitude in human INs (human: 258.8 ± 272.8 pA; rat: 75.8 ± 58.7 pA; p<0.001, MW U-test, Figure 1C and G)
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings showing statistically significant difference (p<0.001).

claim: Human and rat unitary EPSCs have similar latencies.
source: Unitary EPSCs in human and rats had similar latencies (human: 1.04 ± 0.4 ms, n= 37; rat: 1.1 ± 0.38 ms, n = 25; p = 0.79, MW U-test)
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings showing no significant difference (p = 0.79).

claim: Human and rat unitary EPSCs have similar rise times.
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings showing no significant difference (p = 0.95).

claim: Human and rat unitary EPSCs have similar decay times.
source: decay (37%, human: 1.46 ± 0.83 ms, n = 38; rat: 1.7 ± 0.8 ms, n = 26; P = 0.18, MW U-test) times
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings showing no significant difference (p = 0.18).

claim: Human unitary EPSCs have significantly larger charge compared to rats.
source: the larger amplitude with similar decay resulted in a significantly larger EPSC charge in human (human: 553.6 ± 593.3 fC, n=38; rat: 123.1 ± 107.6 fC, n = 26; p<0.001, MW U-test; Figure 1I)
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings showing statistically significant difference (p<0.001).

claim: The number of light microscopy detected synaptic contacts is similar between human and rat pyramidal cell to fast-spiking interneuron connections.
source: Comparison of the number of LM detected synaptic contacts (Nlm) between human (3.3 ± 1.5; range: 1–6) and rat (2.9 ± 1.5, range: 1–6) revealed no significant difference (p = 0.35, MW U-test, Figure 2F)
evidence: Supported by light microscopy reconstruction data showing no significant difference (p = 0.35).

claim: Human active zones are on average twice as large as rat active zones.
source: First we compared the size of presynaptic AZs and found that both human and rat active zones (AZs) have variable sizes (human: 0.02–0.26 μm2; rat: 0.02–0.08 μm2), but the human AZs were on average twice as large (Figure 3P)
evidence: Supported by EM reconstruction data showing human AZ area of 0.077 ± 0.051 μm2 vs rat 0.041 ± 0.017 μm2 (p = 0.002).

claim: Human presynaptic terminals have significantly larger number of docked vesicles per active zone compared to rats.
source: When we counted docked vesicles in these AZs using the 20 nm thin serial section approach we found a significantly larger number in human (4.2 ± 2.2 / AZ) compared to rats (1.3 ± 0.8 / AZ; p<0.001, MW U-test; Figure 3Q)
evidence: Supported by EM serial section data showing statistically significant difference (p<0.001).

claim: Human presynaptic terminals have twice as large docked vesicle density compared to rats.
source: resulting in a twice as large docked vesicle density in human (Figure 3R)
evidence: Supported by EM data showing human density of 58.5 ± 24.6 / μm2 vs rat 32.5 ± 19.9 / μm2 (p < 0.001) from serial sections, and confirmed by EM tomography.

claim: The number of docked vesicles shows a positive correlation with the active zone area in both human and rat.
source: The large variability in the AZ area and number of docked vesicle prompted us to investigate their relationship and found a positive correlation between these parameters in both species (Figure 3S; human: ρ = 0.71; rat: ρ= 0.54, Spearman correlation)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of EM data showing positive Spearman correlation coefficients.

claim: Human axonal boutons have significantly larger volumes compared to rats.
source: Furthermore, we found significantly larger bouton volumes in humans (0.14 ± 0.09 µm3, n = 20) compared to rats (0.05 ± 0.02 µm3, n = 17; p<0.01, MW U-test; Figure 3—figure supplement 1B)
evidence: Supported by EM reconstruction data showing statistically significant difference (p<0.01).

claim: Each bouton contained only a single active zone in both species.
source: Each bouton contained only a single AZ in both species.
evidence: Supported by EM reconstruction observations.

claim: EPSC failure rates were significantly lower in human neurons compared to rats in each calcium condition.
source: EPSC failure rates were significantly lower in human neurons (p<0.012, MW U-test; Figure 2B and D) in each condition compared to rats ([Ca2+]o: 1 mM: 15.8 ± 18.7% vs. 62.8 ± 34.2%, 1.5 mM: 2.0 ± 4.0% vs. 39.1 ± 24.7%, 2 mM: 0 vs. 26.6 ± 21.7%, 4 mM: 0 vs. 8.4 ± 10.2%)
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings showing statistically significant differences (p<0.012) across all calcium conditions.

claim: There is a significant difference in release probability between human and rat at 1.5 mM calcium.
source: We found significant difference in Pr(at 1.5 mM [Ca2+]o: human: 0.33 ± 0.10, range: 0.18–0.48, n = 7; rat: 0.17 ± 0.13, range: 0.05–0.53, n = 12; p = 0.01, MW U-test)
evidence: Supported by MPFA analysis showing statistically significant difference (p = 0.01).

claim: Human slices were derived from non-pathological samples of cortical tissue resected during surgery.
source: Acute brain slices were prepared from small blocks of non-pathological samples of human cortical tissue resected in surgery from female (n = 15, aged 53 ± 13 years) and male (n = 11, aged 43 ± 24 years) patients (Komlosi et al., 2012; Molnar et al., 2008)
evidence: Stated in the methods section describing the source of human tissue samples.

claim: Rat slices were prepared from somatosensory cortex of juvenile rats and prefrontal cortex of adult rats.
source: from somatosensory cortex of juvenile (P18 - 28, n = 9) and prefrontal cortex of adult (P53 - 65, n = 17) male rats using standard acute slice preparation procedures (Olah et al., 2007)
evidence: Stated in the methods section describing the source of rat tissue samples.

claim: No significant differences were found in EPSC charge values between experiments performed in slices from frontal and temporal lobes.
source: We found no significant differences between EPSC charge values between experiments performed in slices prepared from frontal and temporal lobes (425.8 ± 426.7 vs. 760.6 ± 761.2, p = 0.1, MW U-test)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of electrophysiological data showing no significant difference (p = 0.1).

claim: No significant differences were found in EPSC charge between morphologically identified basket and axo-axonic cell groups.
source: and between morphologically identified basket and axo-axonic cell groups (567.5 ± 451.6 vs. 364.9 ± 193.3, p = 0.36, MW U-test)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of electrophysiological data showing no significant difference (p = 0.36).

claim: No significant differences were found in EPSC parameters measured in female and male patients.
source: Furthermore, we found no significant differences in EPSC parameters measured in female and male patients (charge, female: 602.49 ± 480.81 fC, male: 499.27 ± 708.32 fC,p =0.13; rise time, female: 0.46 ± 0.20 ms, male: 0.42 ± 0.13 ms, p = 0.71; decay time, female:1.32 ± 0.56 ms, male:1.63 ± 1.04, p = 0.65, latency female:1.08 ± 0.46 ms, male: 0.99 ± 0.37 ms, p = 0.7, MW U-test)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of electrophysiological data showing no significant differences across all measured parameters.

claim: No correlation was found between the age of patients and EPSC charge, rise time, latency, and decay time.
source: In addition, we found no correlation between the age of patients and the charge (ρ = 0.05, p = 0.76), rise time (ρ = 0, p = 0.99), latency (ρ = 0.16, p = 0.32) and decay (ρ = 0.01, P = 0.94) of the measured EPSCs (Spearman correlation, Figure 1—figure supplement 1)
evidence: Supported by Spearman correlation analysis showing no significant correlations.

claim: No significant differences were found in EPSC charge values between juvenile and adult rat groups.
source: We found no significant differences in EPSC charge values between the two rodent groups (81.6 ± 59.3 vs. 72.7 ± 60.0, p = 0.91, MW U-test)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of electrophysiological data showing no significant difference (p = 0.91).

claim: The docked vesicle density and the size of the proximal vesicle pool normalized to the AZ area showed no significant correlation in human samples.
source: Moreover, the docked vesicle density and the size of the proximal vesicle pool normalized to the AZ area in axon terminals (n = 15 from both species, for definition see Methods) showed no significant correlation both in human (ρ = 0.15, P = 0.59, Spearman correlation)
evidence: Supported by Spearman correlation analysis showing no significant correlation (p = 0.59).

claim: The docked vesicle density and the size of the proximal vesicle pool normalized to the AZ area showed no significant correlation in rat samples.
source: and rat samples (ρ = −0.09, p = 0.76; Figure 3—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: Supported by Spearman correlation analysis showing no significant correlation (p = 0.76).

claim: The 'one site-one vesicle' hypothesis is consistent with rat pyramidal cell active zones containing on average a single functional release site.
source: Our data demonstrating that an AZ in rat PC axons contains on average a single functional release site is consistent with the 'one site-one vesicle' hypothesis (Korn et al., 1982)
evidence: Inference based on experimental data compared to established hypothesis, with citation to Korn et al., 1982.

claim: Multivesicular release is the main mode of operation in human pyramidal cell to fast-spiking interneuron connections.
source: In contrast, the same type of axon terminals in human contain on average 6 functional release sites, demonstrating that here multivesicular release (MVR; (Rudolph et al., 2015) is the main mode of operation.
evidence: Inference based on experimental data showing 6 release sites per AZ, with citation to Rudolph et al., 2015.

claim: The average docking site occupancy is 0.8 in rats.
source: Comparison of the Nfrs and the number of docked vesicles allowed the calculation of the average docking site occupancy that is 0.8 in rats
evidence: Calculated from the ratio of docked vesicles to functional release sites.

claim: The average docking site occupancy is ~0.7 in human synapses.
source: Comparison of the Nfrs and the number of docked vesicles allowed the calculation of the average docking site occupancy that is 0.8 in rats and ~0.7 in human synapses
evidence: Calculated from the ratio of docked vesicles to functional release sites.

claim: The docking site occupancy in human and rat synapses is similar to that calculated for the Calyx of Held.
source: similar to that calculated for the Calyx of Held (Neher, 2010)
evidence: Comparison to published data with citation to Neher, 2010.

claim: The docking site occupancy in human and rat synapses is somewhat higher than that found in cerebellar interneuron synapses.
source: and somewhat higher than that found in cerebellar IN synapses (Pulido et al., 2015)
evidence: Comparison to published data with citation to Pulido et al., 2015.

claim: Similar docking site occupancy and vesicle release probability between human and rodents predict similar short-term plasticity of transmission.
source: Similarly large docking site occupancy and vesicle Pr between human and rodents predict similar short-term plasticity of transmission, a key feature of synapses of dynamic neuronal networks
evidence: Inference based on the calculated docking site occupancy and release probability values.

claim: Human connections have an additional tuning range for connection strength due to higher number of functional release sites.
source: with an additional tuning range for human connection strength due to higher Nfrs
evidence: Inference based on the higher Nfrs in human synapses.

claim: Classic theories link cognitive abilities to synaptic properties.
source: However, classic theories suggest that synaptic properties also contribute to cognitive abilities (Bliss and Lomo, 1973; Buzsaki, 2015; Hebb, 1949; Singer, 1995)
evidence: Statement supported by citations to classic theories.

claim: Human cortical pyramidal cell to pyramidal cell connections display spike timing-dependent long-term plasticity similar to that found in rodents, but with altered plasticity-inducing activity patterns.
source: Human cortical PC to PC connections display spike timing-dependent long-term plasticity similar to that found in rodents, but with altered plasticity-inducing activity patterns (Verhoog et al., 2013)
evidence: Statement supported by citation to Verhoog et al., 2013.

claim: Individual presynaptic action potentials in human pyramidal cells can result in suprathreshold postsynaptic responses in GABAergic neurons.
source: It has also been demonstrated that the outputs of human PCs can be so powerful that individual presynaptic action potentials result in suprathreshold postsynaptic responses in GABAergic neurons and polysynaptic series of events downstream in the network (Komlosi et al., 2012; Molnar et al., 2008)
evidence: Statement supported by citations to Komlosi et al., 2012 and Molnar et al., 2008.

claim: Powerful pyramidal cell to interneuron connections are not characteristic of nonhuman tissue.
source: These powerful PC to IN connections are not characteristic to nonhuman tissue and were speculated to be important in reliable propagation of information in the human neocortex (Woodruff and Yuste, 2008)
evidence: Statement with citation to Woodruff and Yuste, 2008, involving speculation about functional importance.

claim: Similar types of cortical GABAergic interneurons, pyramidal cells and comparable local synaptic connectivity patterns were reported in rodent and human neocortices.
source: For example, similar types of cortical GABAergic interneurons (INs), pyramidal cells (PCs) and comparable local synaptic connectivity patterns were reported in rodent and human neocortices (Molnar et al., 2008; Olah et al., 2007; Yanez et al., 2005)
evidence: Statement supported by citations to Molnar et al., 2008; Olah et al., 2007; Yanez et al., 2005.

claim: There are species-specific differences in layering, long-range connections and intrinsic electrical and morphological properties of nerve cells between human and rodent.
source: Although, there are species-specific differences in the layering, long-range connections and intrinsic electrical and morphological properties of nerve cells (Mohan et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2015)
evidence: Statement supported by citations to Mohan et al., 2015 and Wang et al., 2015.

claim: Multivesicular release is not a human-specific feature of cortical synapses, but is expected to occur at large active zones in rats.
source: Thus, MVR is not a human-specific feature of cortical synapses, but it is expected to occur at large AZs of this connection in rats, as it has been shown to take place in many other rat glutamatergic synapses (Rudolph et al., 2015)
evidence: Inference based on the correlation between AZ size and docked vesicles, with citation to Rudolph et al., 2015.

claim: Scalability of multivesicular release in human synapses as opposed to all-or-none single vesicular rat synapses provides additional functional variability.
source: Even if upscaling of release components simply follows larger neurons and synapses in the human microcircuit, it is important to note that scalability of multivesicular release in human synapses as opposed to all-or-none single vesicular rat synapses provides additional functional variability, which might subserve evolutionary optimization.
evidence: Inference and speculation about functional implications of the observed differences.

claim: Strong connections linking pyramidal cells and select postsynaptic neurons could be strategically positioned for the emergence and maintenance of key cortical hubs characteristic of the human cerebral cortex.
source: The strong connections linking pyramidal cells and a select group of postsynaptic neurons in the same area of the neocortex could be strategically positioned for the emergence and maintenance of key cortical hubs characteristic of the human cerebral cortex (Haggmann et al. 2008)
evidence: Speculation about functional implications with citation to Haggmann et al. 2008.

claim: Long-range connections of pyramidal cells with strong local connections might provide structural and functional basis for the formation of small world networks important in linking connections to cognition.
source: Long-range connections of PCs with strong local connections might also target distant INs with similarly powerful unitary EPSPs speculatively providing structural and functional basis for the formation of small world networks suggested to be important in linking connections to cognition (Park and Friston, 2013)
evidence: Speculation about functional implications with citation to Park and Friston, 2013.

claim: The space that harbors a functional release site or a docking site is substantially smaller in human active zones compared to rats.
source: Thus, the space that harbors a functional release site or a docking site seems to be substantially smaller in human AZs.
evidence: Inference based on the calculated area per release site (0.012 μm2 in human vs 0.025 μm2 in rat).

claim: Answering why the molecular machinery necessary for the assembly of a functional release site needs less space in human requires quantitative proteomic analysis of active zones at nanometer resolutions.
source: This raises an interesting question: why the molecular machinery necessary for the assembly of a functional release site needs less space in human? Answering this question requires quantitative proteomic analysis of these AZs at nanometer resolutions.
evidence: Speculation about future research directions needed to answer the question.

claim: Reconstructions from very thin serial EM sections provide a reliable measure of the number of docked vesicles.
source: These results confirmed that reconstructions from very thin serial EM sections also provide a reliable measure of the number of docked vesicles.
evidence: Inference based on comparison between serial EM and EM tomography results showing similar two-fold differences.

claim: EM tomography is the best currently known method for precise identification of docked vesicles.
source: However, as the precise identification of docked vesicles is challenging in conventional EM even if very thin (20 nm) sections are used, we repeated these measurements using EM tomography; the best currently known method for this application (Imig et al., 2014; Siksou et al., 2007)
evidence: Statement supported by citations to Imig et al., 2014 and Siksou et al., 2007.

claim: Human slices were derived from frontal, temporal, and parietal regions.
source: Human slices were derived from material that had to be removed to gain access for the surgical treatment of deep-brain tumors from the left and right frontal (n = 22), temporal (n = 14), and parietal (n = 3) regions
evidence: Description of the tissue source in the methods section.

claim: Postsynaptic interneurons were identified as either axo-axonic cells or basket cells based on their characteristic axonal morphology.
source: Postsynaptic INs were identified as either axo-axonic (AACs, human: n = 6) or basket (BCs, human: n = 18; rat: n = 8) cells based on their characteristic axonal cartridges or axonal branches forming perisomatic baskets, respectively (Klausberger and Somogyi, 2008; Figure 1B and F)
evidence: Description of cell identification method with citation to Klausberger and Somogyi, 2008.

claim: Human basket cells and axo-axonic cells have similar dendritic arbor lengths.
source: Reconstructions allowed the measurement of the length of dendritic (BCs, n = 9, 2912 ± 1076 µm; AACs, n = 5, 2897 ± 1546 µm, p = 1, MW U-test)
evidence: Supported by morphological reconstruction data showing no significant difference (p = 1).

claim: Human basket cells and axo-axonic cells have similar axonal arbor lengths.
source: and axonal (BCs, n = 7, 27,489 ± 14,080 µm; AACs, n = 5, 20732 ± 3332 µm, p = 0.41) arbors within our human slices
evidence: Supported by morphological reconstruction data showing no significant difference (p = 0.41).

claim: NMDA receptor antagonist was used during MPFA to prevent NMDA channel openings that might reduce variances and induce long-term plasticity.
source: These recordings were performed in the presence of an NMDA and a cannabinoid receptor antagonist (20 μM D-AP-5 and 10 μM AM251, respectively) to prevent NMDA channel openings, which might reduce variances and induce long-term plasticity (Silver, 2003; Saviane and Silver, 2007)
evidence: Methodological justification with citations to Silver, 2003 and Saviane and Silver, 2007.

claim: Cannabinoid receptor antagonist was used during MPFA to exclude retrograde short- or long-term modification of glutamatergic transmission.
source: and to exclude undesirable retrograde short- or long-term modification of glutamatergic transmission (Lee et al. 2010, Péterfi et al. 2012) during MPFA
evidence: Methodological justification with citations to Lee et al. 2010 and Péterfi et al. 2012.

claim: The low affinity competitive non-NMDA receptor antagonist γDGG was included to prevent AMPA receptor saturation.
source: The low affinity competitive non-NMDA receptor antagonist γDGG (0.5 mM) was included to prevent AMPA receptor saturation (Sakaba et al., 2002; Scheuss et al., 2002; Wadiche and Jahr, 2001)
evidence: Methodological justification with citations to Sakaba et al., 2002; Scheuss et al., 2002; Wadiche and Jahr, 2001.

claim: L-glutamate was added to the presynaptic internal solution to avoid rundown of EPSCs during long-lasting recordings.
source: To avoid rundown of EPSCs during long-lasting recordings, 10 mM L-glutamate was added to the internal solution of the presynaptic cell (Biro et al., 2005; Ishikawa et al., 2002)
evidence: Methodological justification with citations to Biro et al., 2005 and Ishikawa et al., 2002.

claim: Control experiments showed no significant decrease in EPSC amplitude or charge during long recordings up to 90 minutes.
source: In order to exclude unwanted decrease of EPSC amplitudes during long recordings, we performed control experiments on pyramidal cell to basket cell pairs (n = 5). During these experiments we used the same configuration to assess possible rundown effects. We made at least 50 min-long recordings (up to 90 min) with inter-event intervals of 5 s. We found no significant decrease in the amplitude or charge between epochs selected from the first and last part of recordings (50 traces, charge: p≥0.41; amplitude: p≥0.21, unpaired t-test)
evidence: Supported by control experiment data showing no significant changes.

claim: The human cerebral cortex is considered to be one of the most complex biological structures.
source: The human cerebral cortex is considered to be one of the most complex biological structures, endowing us to perform sophisticated cognitive tasks.
evidence: Statement reflecting established scientific knowledge.
